document.title: Motion for Leave to Answer and Limited Answer of the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners in response to certain parties' responses to the 04/24/2026 Answer

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.   
 
)  
 
Docket No. ER26-1479-000 
 
MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND LIMITED ANSWER OF  
THE INDICATED PJM TRANSMISSION OWNERS 
 
Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy 
Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”), 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212 and 385.213, the 
Indicated PJM Transmission Owners1 submit this Limited Answer in response to certain parties’ 
responses to the PJM Transmission Owners’ April 24, 2026 answer submitted regarding PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) 60-Day Compliance Filing in the above-captioned proceeding.2  
This answer is limited to addressing replies to the PJM Transmission Owners on the issue of PJM’s 
proposed modifications to retail Behind the Meter-Generation (“Retail BTMG”) rules, in 
compliance with the Commission’s December 18, 2025 Order in this proceeding (“December 18 
 
1  
For purposes of this filing, the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners are: American Electric Power Service 
Corporation on behalf of its affiliates, Appalachian Power Company, Indiana Michigan Power Company, Kentucky 
Power Company, Kingsport Power Company, Ohio Power Company, Wheeling Power Company, AEP Appalachian 
Transmission Company, Inc. AEP Indiana Michigan Transmission Company, Inc., AEP Kentucky Transmission 
Company, Inc., AEP Ohio Transmission Company, Inc., and AEP West Virginia Transmission Company, Inc.; The 
Dayton Power and Light Company d/b/a AES Ohio; Dominion Energy Services, Inc. on behalf of Virginia Electric 
and Power Company d/b/a Dominion Energy Virginia; Duke Energy Business Services, LLC for Duke Energy 
Kentucky, Inc. and Duke Energy Ohio, Inc.; Duquesne Light Company; East Kentucky Power Cooperative; Exelon 
Corporation on behalf of its affiliates Atlantic City Electric Company, Baltimore Gas and Electric Company, 
Commonwealth Edison Company, Commonwealth Edison Company of Indiana, Inc., Delmarva Power & Light 
Company, PECO Energy Company, and Potomac Electric Power Company; FirstEnergy Service Company, on behalf 
of its affiliates American Transmission Systems, Incorporated, Jersey Central Power & Light Company, Mid-Atlantic 
Interstate Transmission LLC, The Potomac Edison Company, Monongahela Power Company, Keystone Appalachian 
Transmission Company, and Trans-Allegheny Interstate Line Company (collectively, the “FirstEnergy Companies”); 
PPL Electric Utilities Corporation; Public Service Electric and Gas Company; Rockland Electric Company; and the 
Southern Maryland Electric Cooperative (“PJM Transmission Owners”). 
2  
To the extent required, the PJM Transmission Owners respectfully move for leave to answer.  The 
Commission’s procedural rules generally prohibit answers to answers.  However, the Commission has the discretion 
to waive its prohibition of answers to answers for good cause shown, i.e., to assist the Commission’s understanding 
and resolution of the issues raised or to ensure a complete record.  See, e.g., Pioneer Transmission, LLC v. N. Ind. 
Pub. Serv. Co., 140 FERC ¶ 61,057, at P 94 (2012); Midwest Indep. Transmission Sys. Operator, Inc., 120 FERC ¶ 
61,083, at P 23 (2007); Morgan Stanley Cap. Grp., Inc. v. N.Y. Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 93 FERC ¶ 61,017, at 
61,036 (2000); CNG Transmission Corp., 89 FERC ¶ 61,100, at 61,287 n.11 (1999).  This Answer is submitted to 
ensure a complete and accurate record.  Accordingly, good cause exists to permit this answer.

2 
Order”),3 specifically the level of materiality threshold for Retail BTMG, as well as the proposed 
grandfathering provisions to ensure that existing Retail BTMG arrangements are not unfairly 
harmed by the transition to the new Retail BTMG rules required by the December 18 Order.4  For 
the reasons explained below, the Commission should reject arguments for a materiality threshold 
greater than 50 MW, while ensuring that grandfathering provisions are appropriately robust to 
avoid unfair impacts to existing customers that have substantially relied on PJM’s Retail BTMG 
rules. 
I. 
ANSWER  
In their April 24 answer, the PJM Transmission Owners explained that the Commission 
should reject arguments arguing for a Retail BTMG threshold higher than 50 MW because the 50 
MW threshold strikes the appropriate balance between allowing continued use of Retail BTMG 
with the appropriate limitations to ensure reliability.  In response, the Answering Parties contend 
that 50 MW is “arbitrarily low” and would include facilities that pose no reliability risk to PJM.5  
These arguments broadly miss the point: the issue is less that existing Retail BTMG arrangements 
create substantial reliability risks on their own, but rather that the proliferation of large loads, 
including those that opt to utilize arrangements with on-site generation, pose an increasing risk 
due to the fact that Retail BTMG are not fully accounted for in resource adequacy planning and 
can shift costs onto other transmission customers contrary to cost causation principles.6   
 
3  
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217, at PP 179, 221-224 (2025).   
4  
Specifically, the PJM Transmission Owners reply to the further answers filed by Eastman Chemical 
Company (“Eastman”), the PJM Industrial Customer Coalition (“Industrials”), and the BTMG Parties (collectively, 
“Answering Parties”). 
5  
Eastman at 3; Industrials at 3-4. 
6  
December 18 Order at P 186.

3 
These were the concerns underlying the Commission’s finding that PJM’s existing Retail 
BTMG arrangements are no longer just and reasonable, with the Commission specifically agreeing 
with PJM’s explanation that the existing BTMG rules were conceived and implemented for 
substantially smaller loads, and that problems could occur if large loads were allowed to use the 
existing BTMG rules.7  Although Commission did not make a finding as to a particular just and 
reasonable materiality threshold in the December 18 Order, it did note as “points of reference” that 
PJM requires individual metering for generators above 10 MW and that the Commission’s 
definition of a small generator is 20 MW.8  In this light, PJM’s 50 MW threshold is entirely 
reasonable, as it is high enough to exempt substantially-sized commercial and industrial facilities, 
but is not so high as to create ongoing reliability risks as well as shifting an unreasonable amount 
of costs to other ratepayers.  The need to avoid cost-shifting is particularly apt given concerns over 
ratepayer affordability and subsidization, which will only increase as more large loads come 
online.  For these reasons, the Commission should accept PJM’s 50 MW threshold. 
The Commission should also reject arguments that PJM failed to comply with the 
December 18 Order because it proposed a Retail BTMG materiality threshold based on generation 
capacity rather than load size.  As PJM explained, it reasonably based the threshold on generator 
size—measured by cumulative nameplate rating—because generator capacity is static and 
administrable, whereas load can fluctuate.9  None of the Answering Parties adequately address this 
point, instead focusing on the reference to the “amount of load” in the December 18 Order, 
particularly in Ordering Paragraph (F).10  However, that Ordering Paragraph made clear that PJM’s

compliance obligation was “as discussed in the body” of the December 18 Order.  In discussing 
potentially appropriate thresholds in the body of the December 18 Order, the Commission did not 
preclude a generation-based threshold.  To the contrary, the Commission specifically provided two 
points of reference based on generator size, rather than the size of load itself.  Answering Parties’ 
contentions that PJM’s proposal conflicts with the December 18 Order are therefore without 
merit.11 
Finally, it is clear from Answering Parties arguments that their primary concern involves 
the treatment of existing Retail BTMG customers, rather than new large loads.  The PJM 
Transmission Owners agree it is important that an appropriate materiality threshold rule should be 
paired with grandfathering provisions recognizing that industrial and commercial customers have 
relied on Retail BTMG rules.  To that end, the PJM Transmission Owners indicated their support 
for certain additions and clarifications to PJM’s grandfathering proposal suggested by Answering 
Parties, and other commenters.  The PJM Transmission Owners are open to additional suggestions 
as well as the development of further detail regarding the implementation of the grandfathering 
provisions in order to avoid substantial financial harm to existing Retail BTMG customers.  
However, the need for robust grandfathering provisions is not a convincing reason to increase the 
materiality threshold going forward.  The two mechanisms address fundamentally different 
concerns—the grandfathering provisions are meant to protect existing customers that have relied 
on existing BTMG rules, while the materiality threshold is intended to ensure that the proliferation 
of new large loads does not compromise reliability or shift costs to other PJM ratepayers.  The 
Commission should reject the attempts of the Answering Parties to conflate the two issues. 
 
 
11  
December 18 Order at P 221.

5 
II. 
CONCLUSION 
The PJM Transmission Owners respectfully request that the Commission accept this 
answer and that any subsequent Commission orders addressing these issues be consistent with the 
discussion herein. 
 
Respectfully Submitted,
